newsitem.title: USA: Nationwide's expansion plan disappoints housing group.
newsitem.headline: Nationwide's expansion plan disappoints housing group.

text.p: Nationwide Insurance, hit by allegations that it has discriminated against minorities, announced plans Friday to revise underwriting guidelines and expand its investment in the nation's cities.

Nationwide, which has been in talks with the Justice Department over the allegations, said it will make an initial investment of $3 million in urban areas and open new sales and service offices in Baltimore, Cleveland and Philadelphia.

Columbus, Ohio-based Nationwide, the nation's sixth largest property-casualty insurer, said it will drop restrictions on the age and minimum market value of the properties it will insure in its underwriting guidelines.
In addition, replacement cost coverage will now be available to all Nationwide customers.
But the housing group that leveled the accusations of discrimination against Nationwide said it was disappointed with the measures.

"This company is doing too little, too late," said Shanna Smith, executive director of the non-profit National Fair Housing Alliance, which claims Nationwide makes it difficult or costly for homeowners in some predominantly black, Hispanic or integrated neighbourhoods to insure their homes.

"We're really pretty disappointed because what they kept in place was their geographic-based marketing programme," Smith said, adding that it was "designed to discourage agents from doing business in urban areas."
Nationwide categorically denied the company has engaged in discriminatory practices and said the steps being taken demonstrated a commitment urban markets.
"These new initiatives are going to provide our sales force with every incentive and opportunity to write business in urban markets," a Nationwide spokesman said.
"We believe these changes will allow our businesses to grow in urban markets," he said.

The Fair Housing Alliance also criticised the size of Nationwide's planned urban investment, which falls short of a $14.5 million settlement agreed to by another insurer, American Family Insurance Co., in 1995.
But Nationwide's investment, taken on its own and not as part of a legal settlement, exceeded State Farm's $1 million resolution of similar complaints last year.
In addition, Nationwide said similar investments will be made in other cities as Nationwide expands its urban presence.

"As we strive to strengthen our position as a leading insurance provider, the urban market represents an attractive source of business," said Richard Crabtree, president of Nationwide's property and casualty insurance companies.
"Serving this market effectively, while working to strengthen urban neighbourhoods is a crucial part of Nationwide's business strategy," Crabtree said.
Nationwide said the urban marketing plan grew out of a broader initiative from 1994 to focus on better serving customers and improving its competitive position.
Nationwide said the first phase of the plan included a massive restructuring of field operations and consolidation of processing operations.
